label: DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017
output:
**The Coolroom Died and Somehow It Was Our Best Service: A Cup Day Letter to Jonno**

Jonno,

Right. You keep messaging me about the coolroom and I keep saying I’ll tell you later, and then I finish a double and my thumbs stop working, so I’m doing this instead. This is the long version. Send it to yourself, print it out, read it on the Tube like a proper little London wanker. Mum, if you’re reading this, sorry about the language. It’s Jonno’s fault.

So. Cup Week. Tuesday 3 November, Cup Day proper. I’m on the early open, rock up at some ungodly hour, and the first thing I notice is that the kitchen smells wrong. Not “someone left the mop in the bucket” wrong. Proper wrong. I open the coolroom and the thermometer says 11 degrees. Eleven. That’s not a coolroom, that’s a slightly chilly lounge room. The compressor had carked it overnight, sometime between Monday night and Tuesday morning, and nobody knew because the coolroom doesn’t bloody text you, does it.

We had 140 covers booked for Cup Day lunch. Set menu, three courses. The kind of day where people book in August and wear a stupid hat and expect the duck to be perfect. And I’m standing there at 6.40am looking at a dead coolroom like it’s personally wronged me.

Rang Wally from Coldline. Good bloke, but he’s booked out and the part’s coming from Sydney, so he can’t get to us till Wednesday. Wednesday. On Cup Day. Great. Love that. The owner, Phil, does his usual thing of saying, “Just make it work, mate.” Phil, mate, “make it work” is not a plan. It’s a vibe. It’s what you say when you don’t want to be on the phone anymore. I love Phil, but if “just make it work” was a trade, we’d all be fucked.

Raff was off Cup Day, so it was me running the kitchen. Benny on pans, Kev on dish, and a couple of casuals who looked at me like I was going to say the building was on fire. Honestly, for about ten minutes, I considered it.

First move: get everything out of the dead coolroom. We shifted what we could into the two undercounters, the bar fridge, and Marta next door let us use half her walk-in. Marta runs the cafe down the side and she’s an actual angel, but she’s also a businesswoman. She made us pay her back in croissant credit. I owe her about three weeks of staff meal now. Every time I see her she goes, “How’s my croissant debt going?” I’m considering just moving into her walk-in and paying rent in butter.

We lost about $1,800 of stock. Mostly dairy and the duck legs. The duck legs hurt. Not emotionally, because I’m not going to sit here and do a sob story about poultry, but they were nice duck legs and they died for nothing.

Then there was the beef shin. Thirty kilos of it, still in the far coolroom over the laneway, because of course it was. So me and Benny put it on a milk crate trolley and wheeled it down the laneway in the rain. One wheel fell off halfway. Not slowly, either. Just bailed. So I’m carrying one end of a milk crate trolley with 30kg of beef shin on it, in the rain, in my whites, while Benny’s going, “We’re fine, we’re fine,” which is what people say when they are absolutely not fine.

Kev, our dishy, saved the day in the most Kev way possible. He fucked off to the servo and came back with 14 bags of ice for the old esky. The servo guy asked if we were having a party. Kev said, “Yeah, mate. A beef party.” Legend. He’s 19 and he’s got more situational awareness than half the chefs I’ve worked with.

Service itself was chaos, but the good kind. We had to 86 the panna cotta at 12.15, which is early, even for us. So dessert became “affogato with whatever” and people loved it more? I don’t understand customers. I really don’t. We could have served them a shoe with a scoop of vanilla and they’d have put it on Instagram. The lady on table 9 asked if the beef was “free range from the laneway” because she saw us out the window with the trolley. I said, “Yeah, love, it’s laneway-aged.” She nodded like that was a real thing. I’ve been thinking about it for a week.

My horse in the sweep was called Ice Cold Lad. Came second last. The universe is taking the piss. I don’t know what I expected. I picked it because of the coolroom. That’s not a strategy, that’s a cry for help.

But here’s the thing, and I know you’ll hate this because you’re soft now: it was honestly the best service we’ve done all year. Everyone was locked in. No one whinged, no one stood around, Benny was calling tickets like his life depended on it, Kev was running ice and plates and doing that thing where he says “heard” before you’ve even finished the sentence. Even the casuals stopped looking terrified and started looking like they might actually work in kitchens. We were down a coolroom, down a chef, down a trolley wheel, and somehow the whole thing clicked. Bistro kitchens run on bar fridges and spite. That’s the industry secret. You can keep your fancy London induction hobs. Give me a bar fridge, a milk crate, and a dishy who knows where the servo is.

Now. You. Jonno. You used to be on grill with me. You were there for the Great Sink Blockage of 2024. You know what a bad service looks like. And yet you’ve been messaging me from London like you’ve forgotten how a kitchen works. “What happened with the coolroom?” What do you think happened, mate? It died. We panicked. We put beef in a trolley. We served affogato with whatever.

London has made you soft. You probably own a tote bag now. You probably say “flat white” in a little voice. If you’d been there, you’d have cried. Not a little cry either. A proper sit-down-on-the-milk-crate cry. You’d have asked Wally if he could come via Zoom. You’d have tried to laminate a risk assessment. You’d have called the panna cotta “a deconstructed affogato opportunity” and then gone for a vape.

You would have lost your mind. And honestly, I wish you’d been there. Not because you’d have helped, but because I’d have loved to watch your face when the wheel fell off.

So yeah. That’s the coolroom story. It’s funny now. It was less funny at 6.40am on Cup Day when I was staring at a thermometer and doing maths in my head about how many croissants I’d have to owe Marta. But we got through it, we lost some duck legs, and somehow we had a cracking service.

Come home ya flog. The bar fridge misses you.

— Me
